title: Repunit Divisibility: Complete Order-of-10 Characterization
description: A complete biconditional for repunit divisibility: d ∣ R(k) if and only if the multiplicative order of 10 modulo d divides k, provided gcd(d,9)=1. Proves the open question from DivisibilityByThreeOQ02 via a clean ZMod ring identity.

meta.author: Formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib
originalContributions: Complete biconditional: d ∣ R(k) ↔ orderOf(10 : ZMod d) ∣ k
ZMod ring identity: 9·R(k) + 1 = 10^k holds in any ZMod d (proved by induction with linear_combination)
Identifies correct hypothesis: gcd(d,9)=1, NOT gcd(d,10)=1 (d=3 fails the latter condition)
Verified concrete examples: ord_7(10)=6, ord_11(10)=2, ord_13(10)=6, ord_37(10)=3 via native_decide
meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified with 0 axioms and 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: Repunits R(k) = 111...1 (k ones) have been studied since the 19th century. The name 'repunit' was coined by Samuel Yates in 1966 (short for 'repeated unit'). The classical question of which integers divide some repunit is settled by: d ∣ R(k) for some k if and only if gcd(d,10)=1, i.e., d shares no factor with 2 or 5. The more refined question — for a fixed d, which k satisfy d ∣ R(k) — is governed by the multiplicative order of 10 modulo d, a fact connected to the period of the decimal expansion of 1/d. DivisibilityByThreeOQ02.lean proved the simpler direction (d ∣ R(k) ↔ d ∣ 10^k-1 when gcd(d,9)=1) and listed concrete cases. This file proves the complete biconditional, answering the open question from that file.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question from DivisibilityByThreeOQ02.lean**:

Given d with gcd(d,9)=1 and d>1, and a repunit R(k) = 1+10+...+10^(k-1), characterize exactly when d ∣ R(k).

The order-of-10 conjecture: d ∣ R(k) ↔ ord_d(10) ∣ k.
overview.text: d ∣ R(k) if and only if the multiplicative order of 10 modulo d divides k.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Key ring identity**: In any ZMod d (not just when d > 1), one has the exact equation:
$$9 \cdot R(k) + 1 = 10^k \in \mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$$
This is proved by induction with `linear_combination 10 * ih`.

**Forward direction** (d ∣ R(k) → 10^k ≡ 1): If R(k) ≡ 0, then 9·R(k) = 0, so 10^k = 0 + 1 = 1.

**Backward direction** (10^k ≡ 1 → d ∣ R(k)): From the ring identity, 9·R(k) = 10^k - 1 = 0 in ZMod d. This means d ∣ 9·R(k) in ℕ. Since gcd(d,9)=1, `Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left` gives d ∣ R(k).
keyInsights: The identity 9·R(k)+1=10^k holds in ZMod d as a pure ring identity — no need to handle natural number subtraction.
The inductive step uses `linear_combination 10 * ih`, a one-line proof once the ring identity is clear.
The correct coprimality hypothesis is gcd(d,9)=1, not gcd(d,10)=1: d=3 satisfies gcd(3,10)=1 but the theorem fails since ord_3(10)=1 yet 3∤R(1)=1.
The backward direction works over ℕ coprime divisibility, avoiding the need for ZMod units.

The repunit is redefined locally as a `private def` to avoid importing the parent module DivisibilityByThreeOQ02.lean — keeping this file self-contained and preventing duplicate definition conflicts while remaining mathematically identical.

sections.title: §0: Module Docstring and Imports
sections.summary: 18-line module docstring explains the biconditional, key ring identity 9·R(k)+1=10^k, and the gcd(d,9)=1 hypothesis. Three imports: ZMod.Basic, GroupTheory.OrderOfElement, Mathlib.Tactic.
sections.mathContext: The docstring states the characterization d ∣ R(k) ↔ orderOf(10 mod d) ∣ k and notes why gcd(d,9)=1 (not gcd(d,10)=1) is required: d=3 fails the latter condition since ord_3(10)=1 but 3∤R(1)=1.

sections.title: §1: Private Repunit Definition
sections.summary: Self-contained private recursive definition: repunit 0 = 0, repunit (n+1) = repunit n * 10 + 1. Avoids importing the parent module.

sections.title: §2: The ZMod Ring Identity
sections.summary: repunit_ZMod_aux: proves 9·R(k)+1 = 10^k in ZMod d by induction. Key step: simp [repunit] unfolds the recursion, then linear_combination 10*ih closes the goal.
sections.mathContext: This replaces the ℕ-subtraction approach (d ∣ R(k) ↔ d ∣ 10^k-1) with a clean ring identity that works in any ZMod d without natural number overflow.

sections.title: §3: Main Theorem: d ∣ R(k) ↔ orderOf(10) ∣ k
sections.summary: repunit_dvd_iff_orderOf: combines ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff, orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one, the ring identity, and Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left for forward and backward directions.
sections.mathContext: The biconditional reduces to (R(k):ZMod d)=0 ↔ (10:ZMod d)^k=1, handled cleanly in both directions via the ring identity. The backward direction uses gcd(d,9)=1 and Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left to strip the factor of 9.

sections.title: §4: Concrete Verifications
sections.mathContext: These match the orders: ord_7(10)=6, ord_11(10)=2, ord_37(10)=3. Equivalently: $10^6 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$, $10^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$, $10^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{37}$.

crossReferences.description: DivisibilityByThreeOQ02.lean proved repunit_dvd_iff_pow_mod (d∣R(k)↔d∣10^k-1) and listed concrete examples. This file completes the open question with the full orderOf characterization.

conclusion.summary: Complete characterization: d ∣ R(k) ↔ orderOf(10 : ZMod d) ∣ k, for d with gcd(d,9)=1. The proof uses a clean ZMod ring identity 9·R(k)+1=10^k proved by induction with linear_combination.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: This classifies all repunit divisibility in terms of multiplicative orders. For any d with gcd(d,9)=1, the smallest k with d|R(k) is exactly ord_d(10), and more generally d|R(k) iff this order divides k.

**Practical Connection**: The concrete examples verify the well-known orders: ord_7(10)=6 explains why 7|111111 but not 1, 11, 111, 1111, 11111; ord_11(10)=2 explains why 11|11; ord_37(10)=3 explains why 37|111.
openQuestions: Can this be generalized to repunit-like sequences R_b(k) = (b^k-1)/(b-1) for other bases b?
The set of d dividing some repunit is exactly {d : gcd(d,10)=1}. Can this be formally derived from repunit_dvd_iff_orderOf?
